title: How a Diesel’s Cylinder Gets Hot Without Fuel

segments.text: Ever wondered how diesel cylinders heat up before fuel arrives?
During the intake stroke only air—or air mixed with a trace of exhaust gases—enters the cylinder.
The piston then climbs and compresses that air to extreme pressure.
This mechanical work raises the air temperature well above diesel’s ignition point, often past 700 °C.
No fuel is present, so the only energy input is the piston’s motion.
That scorching air becomes the key that triggers spontaneous ignition the moment fuel is injected.
Thus the cylinder’s hot, fuel‑free state sets the stage for power because the air alone creates the heat.
